I am a 63-year-old woman who has farmed these soils in Quzhou for forty years. My body knows the rhythm of this land. With only two mouths in my household and family working off-farm, I cannot waste labor, but my well gives me water when the rains fail, so I sleep soundly.

My wheat-maize rotation is my backbone. I keep **2.1 mu** in that double-cropping system because it feeds us and brings steady cash. The other **2.0 mu** I plant to cotton. Cotton is heavier work—more spraying, more picking—but the price has been decent, and I have managed cotton long enough to know its moods.

For **winter wheat**, I will rotary-till before sowing, as I have always done. I sow an improved variety around National Day. I apply compound fertilizer as a base and top-dress with urea at green-up and jointing. I irrigate three times: after sowing, at jointing, and at grain filling. Wheat pests are mild if you watch carefully; I spray insecticide twice, herbicide once at sowing, and fungicide once if the weather turns damp. I expect about **1,000 jin per mu**—I know my land, and that is honest.

For **summer maize**, I plant immediately after the wheat harvest in early June. I use hybrid seed—everyone here does, and it pays. I do not till for maize; I plant directly into the wheat stubble to save time and fuel, and because the leftover straw keeps moisture. Maize needs less fertilizer than wheat, but I give it enough at planting and once more at the big喇叭口 stage. I irrigate twice, usually at flowering and if August turns dry. I spray insecticide twice and herbicide once. I expect **1,100 jin per mu** in a normal year.

For **cotton**, I rotary-till in April and sow an improved variety like Guoxinmian. Cotton is greedy for potash, so I balance my fertilizer with more K. I irrigate twice, but the real work is pest control—aphids, bollworms, mites. I spray insecticide over ten times through the season, plus herbicide and sometimes a growth regulator. I expect **550 jin of seed cotton per mu**. It is labor, but the income helps when maize prices sag.

I do not chase new fashions. I use what my well, my hands, and forty years of memory tell me is right.

The wheat-maize rotation is my foundation: rotary tillage for wheat, no-tillage for maize to save time after the June harvest, well irrigation three times for wheat and twice for maize, and moderate fertilizer based on forty years of watching these soils. Cotton demands more care—especially fourteen pesticide applications against bollworm and mites—but it diversifies my income.
